Chat and conversation with Llama API

This tutorial introduces you to building conversational applications and question answering systems using Llama API. You will learn the core concepts behind conversational AI and how to implement them effectively for your projects.

Understanding chat completion

Llama API offers a chat completion endpoint that enables you to build sophisticated conversational interfaces. Chat completion is a fundamental capability of large language models (LLMs) that enables natural, interactive conversations. Unlike simple text completion, chat completion maintains the context of a conversation over multiple turns, enabling responses that are more coherent and contextually relevant. The endpoint accepts a sequence of messages, each with a designated role (system, user, or assistant), and generates appropriate responses based on this conversation history.

System messages: System messages provide high-level instructions to the model about how it should behave throughout the conversation. These messages guide the model's overall behavior, tone, and capabilities. For example, you may instruct the model to act as a helpful customer service agent, a language tutor, or a specialized domain expert.

User and assistant messages: User messages represent inputs from your application's users, while assistant messages represent the model's previous responses. By maintaining this sequence of messages, the model can track the conversation flow and generate contextually appropriate responses.

Building conversational applications

Prerequisites: A valid Llama API key; Python 3.7 or higher.

Setting up your environment: To make API calls, set up authentication using your Llama API key, stored in an environment variable. The example imports os, requests, and json, sets LLAMA_API_KEY, and defines BASE_URL = "https://api.llama.com/v1". API keys should be handled securely; avoid hard-coding them.

Discovering available models: Llama API offers a range of models with different capabilities, context lengths, and performance characteristics. Different models offer trade-offs between response quality, latency, and cost. Smaller models respond faster and cost less, larger models often produce higher quality responses. Explore models via the API Playground or query the models endpoint (client.models.list()). In some use cases, deploying multiple models in tandem can be optimal - using powerful models for task-planning and lighter models for execution.

Creating a simple conversation: A conversational application comprises a way to specify prompts and a way to process and display responses. The simplest conversation consists of a system prompt that defines behavior and a user message containing a query. A chat completion request specifies model and messages parameters. The example defines a chat_completion(messages, model, max_tokens) function posting to /chat/completions. The system message isn't required but is often useful guidance.

Building multi-turn conversations: Real-world applications involve multiple turns of dialogue. To create a conversation that flows naturally, maintain the conversation history: append each user message and each model response to the history and send the entire history to the model. A conversation_loop(system_prompt) example maintains conversation state in a list, extracts the assistant content and stop_reason from the response, and appends it back to history.

Memory management for extended conversations: As conversations continue, history grows, leading to challenges:
- Token limits: All models have a maximum context length. Once history exceeds this limit, errors or truncated context occur.
- Cost considerations: Longer prompts consume more tokens and cost more.
- Latency and responsiveness: Longer prompts increase response time.
To address these, implement a sliding window approach: set a maximum number of messages to retain, always keep the system message, and retain only the most recent N messages. A managed_conversation_loop(system_prompt, max_history=10) example keeps the system prompt at index 0 and a window of recent messages. More sophisticated strategies include selective retention (keep important messages by relevance), summarization (periodically summarize older parts), and hierarchical memory (short-term and long-term with different retention policies).

Enhancing user experience with streaming responses: Traditional request-response patterns cause latency. Streaming delivers the response in real-time token-by-token, improving perceived responsiveness, creating a more natural conversation flow, and allowing earlier user processing. Llama API supports streaming through Server-Sent Events (SSE). To implement: set stream to true, process the stream of events, and extract and display each token. The example reads response.iter_lines(), strips the leading "data: " prefix, parses JSON, handles event_type "progress" (appending delta text) and "complete" (breaking).

Summarization and Q&A systems

Understanding text summarization: Text summarization condenses a source text into a shorter version while preserving key information and meaning. Two approaches: extractive summarization (directly extracting important sentences) and abstractive summarization (generating new text capturing the essence). Applications include condensing articles and reports, executive summaries, content previews, and distilling meeting transcripts. The summarize_text function uses a summarization system prompt and the chat completion endpoint.

Customizing summarization with specific instructions: Rather than special parameters, describe the type of summary you want in plain language (prompt engineering). You can control length and verbosity, format and structure, focus and perspective, and tone and style. A custom_summarize(text, instruction) function passes an instruction along with the text.

Building question-answering systems: Q&A systems let users query information using natural language and receive precise answers. The core principle is context-based inference: extracting relevant information from a provided context. This is valuable when users need specific facts, the source is lengthy, or quick precise answers are required. Provide a context document, a question, and instructions; instruct the model to rely solely on the provided context. The answer_question(context, question) function sets a system message to use only the provided context and say so if the answer cannot be determined.

Implementing RAG for enhanced question answering: Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) combines information retrieval with text generation. Rather than relying on a single document, RAG retrieves relevant documents from a larger corpus based on the query, then uses them as context. Advantages: scale across large collections, relevance, factual grounding, and transparency. Production systems use a vector database, semantic search, or a hybrid. The simple_rag_system example uses keyword matching to score and select the top documents, combines them, and calls answer_question. A comprehensive RAG implementation would include document preprocessing and chunking, vector embeddings, efficient vector storage and retrieval, re-ranking, and generation with proper attribution.
completion: A hands-on tutorial for building conversational applications and question-answering systems with Llama API's chat completion endpoint. It explains the role-based message model, system, user, and assistant, that maintains context across turns, then walks through Python setup, secure key handling, and discovering models given their trade-offs in quality, latency, and cost. Readers build progressively: a single-turn request, then a multi-turn loop that appends each exchange to a growing history. To handle long conversations within token, cost, and latency constraints, it introduces a sliding-window memory approach that always retains the system message plus recent messages, and mentions advanced strategies like summarization and hierarchical memory. Tool calling with Llama API

Introduction

You can use tool calling to interface Llama API with external tools that you provide. Tool calling enables you to expand the capabilities of a Llama model in order to gather new information that is not readily available to the model, or to take actions such as sending emails or calling other APIs.

When you enable tool calling via the API, the model automatically decides if it needs one or more of the available tools to respond to your prompt, and if so will tell you which tools it would like to use and how. You will then execute the tool and send back the results as part of a chat completion, so that the model can incorporate the information into its next response.

When to use tool calling

Tool calling can be used for a number of different purposes, which can broadly be grouped as finding information and performing actions.

Finding information: Tool calling enables access to knowledge not included in the model's training data.
- Fetching real-time data: such as sports scores, news headlines, weather data, or the latest stock values.
- Performing calculations: Language models don't perform well with raw arithmetic; create a custom tool for specialized calculations such as tax accounting or internal projections.
- Search the web: Use a search engine to collect additional information as a general solution for fetching real-time data.
- Access databases: Access your own private databases to answer questions about your business or customers, including up-to-date pricing or availability.

Performing actions: Beyond finding information, you can use tools to take actions. Multi-turn actions enable Llama to become a true AI agent.
- Sending messages: Send emails or chat messages proactively.
- Triggering jobs: Start long-running jobs or workflows in the background.
- Calling other APIs: Make API calls to external services.

How to use tool calling

Prerequisites: A valid Llama API key; Python 3.7 or higher.

Setting up your environment: Set up authentication using your Llama API key stored in an environment variable. The example imports os, requests, json, sets LLAMA_API_KEY, and defines BASE_URL = "https://api.llama.com/v1".

Creating a tool definition: The tool (singular) role is a special role that indicates the results come from an external tool. When the model uses a tool, it includes a tool_calls field in the response. After you execute the tool call, return the results using the tool role. A tool definition includes the tool's name, a description of what it does, and the parameters it accepts. The chat completion API accepts a tools parameter (an array of tool definitions), separate from messages. It is not necessary to include tool information in the system prompt or request that the model use tools; if tools are included, the model will by default use them if it decides they are necessary.

The example defines a get_weather tool (with a required location parameter) and calls the chat completion API with a user message "What is the weather in Menlo Park?". The model responds with stop_reason "tool_calls" and a tool_calls array containing the function name get_weather and arguments {"location":"Menlo Park"}, plus token metrics.

Invoking your tool: Llama API does not have access to any execution environment and in many cases will not have access to the tool you defined. Your application must execute the tool call and return the results to the model using the tool role, including the tool_call_id and the content (e.g., {"Menlo Park": "47f"}). Consider using llama-stack-apps or another similar application to execute the tool call. Finally, the model uses the results to return an answer (e.g., "The current temperature in Menlo Park is 47F.") with stop_reason "stop".

Testing & debugging: Because tool calls are executed outside the model, test and debug them separately. For testing you can return a mock response with the expected output, allowing you to experiment with different tools and iterate on tool definitions and prompts before building. Sometimes the model may not call the tool even if available, because it may not believe the tool is the best option. To help the model call the right tool:
- Provide examples of how the tool should be used in the system prompt.
- Modify the tool definition to include more specific instructions or examples.
- If you know the tool should be used, directly ask the model to use the tool in the prompt.

Example tools: Tool definitions are up to you and can be specific or broad. Tools often correspond to a web API or service, but could call a library function or perform a calculation. Examples include a web_search tool (with a query parameter) and a calculate tool using Wolfram Alpha as a calculator (with an expression parameter).

Moderation and security

Overview

Moderation and security are important considerations when building any application, and creating AI applications requires additional considerations that may not be necessary in traditional software development.

Llama models have been trained with safety in mind, and by default they try to avoid generating problematic content. However, various contexts have different content requirements, and your application may need additional or different protection above what the models provide.

Use the moderations endpoints to detect and protect against problematic content as part of an automated moderation system.

Automated moderation

To use the automated moderation tools, you should pass each message to the moderations endpoint before displaying it to the user. This includes both the user's input and the model's generated output. The moderations endpoint will not generate chat completions, so you should pass the user's input to the endpoint separately from the model's output. You can pass in the entire message history to the endpoint, including the system prompt.

A Python example defines run_moderation_check(messages) which posts to https://api.llama.com/v1/moderations and inspects results[0]; if flagged is true it prints the flagged_categories and advises not to send to the model, otherwise it is safe.

You should also verify the model's chat completion response using the moderations endpoint. Even if the user's message is considered safe, checking the model's reply further reduces the likelihood of a problematic response. The example moderates a full message history including a system message, user message, and assistant response.

For applications with strict latency requirements, you may choose to launch a separate thread to run the user-side moderation check in the background while the main thread continues to process the user's message simultaneously. Then wait to display the model's response until the moderation checks have completed.

Designing for mistakes

Like all generative models (and humans), Llama models sometimes make mistakes. It is critical that your system is designed with this fact in mind. Relying on perfect or near-perfect model outputs will only result in undesired outcomes. Instead, design your system to be robust to some amount of error.

A good design pattern is to provide a mechanism that enables the user to "unwind" the model's mistakes, such as an undo button that checks application state prior to the model executing, or a popup that requests user confirmation before making changes. You may also warn users that the model's output could be incorrect, and offer users the ability to give feedback on incorrect outputs.

Adversarial testing

Actively test your system's ability to stay well-behaved under pressure. Adversarial testing (or "red teaming") attempts to deliberately produce incorrect outputs, bypass filters, or otherwise "break" your model. You might pretend to be a user entering invalid or confusing input, or a bad actor looking to misuse your model for profit. An example adversarial prompt asks a customer support bot for a million dollar refund. Adversarial prompts are often saved and reused for regression testing to ensure those failures don't recur.

System prompts

The system prompt is a useful mechanism for guiding Llama's output and can constrain the AI to avoid certain topics or styles. However, do not rely on the system prompt to protect against unsafe outputs, as it is nearly always possible to "jailbreak" the model. Consider the system prompt just one tool to control output. If it is critical not to output certain words or phrases, add hard-coded checks after the model runs. Do not consider your system prompt safely hidden, as it's typically possible to get a model to output its system prompt with adversarial techniques. Do not include sensitive or confidential information in your system prompt, especially secrets such as API keys or passwords.

Attributing API calls to users

Llama API supports adding a unique user identifier for each API call on the chat completion endpoint. You can use this field to attribute API calls to specific users. This identifier can help you identify specific users in the event of Meta-detected API abuse by your end users. Set the user field to a unique string representing the current user (e.g., their user ID). If using usernames or email addresses, hash these before sending to avoid sending personal or identifying information. You should always be able to identify the end user from whatever value you set.

You remain responsible for any legal reporting obligations in relation to your Users and their use of Llama API, and for responding to third-party requests such as from regulators or law enforcement. Where provided by you and detected by Meta, Meta may share the user identifier with you to assist moderation. In line with the API terms of service, Meta may also use the user identifier to promote safety, integrity and security and/or share it with third parties, including law enforcement, to comply with its own legal obligations.

Traditional security practices

It's important not to overlook traditional security practices when building AI applications.

API keys: Store keys securely and do not hard-code them. Never commit API keys to version control, and rotate them immediately if compromised. Limit key access to employees who need them. Separate production keys from developer or staging keys. Consider using a secrets manager.

Running code: A common pattern is to generate code that's executed to complete a task. Follow best practices: use a sandboxed environment, limit permissions of executed code, monitor for suspicious activity (excessive network usage or CPU/GPU load), and restrict the sandbox's internet/network access. Be mindful of how code is generated and especially the prompt used; do not directly place user input into a code-generation prompt, since users may be able to generate and execute arbitrary code. Instead, use a structured approach to generate executable code.

Although Llama models are trained to avoid problematic content, developers often need extra protection, so the guide recommends an automated moderation layer that passes both user input and model output through the moderations endpoint before anything is displayed, with latency advice about running checks on a background thread. It stresses designing for inevitable model mistakes by giving users ways to undo actions, confirm changes, and report errors. Best practices

Overview

The language models available on Llama API are powerful and flexible tools. These guidelines will help you get the most out of Llama API and avoid common pitfalls when working with models.

Prompting

Write clear instructions: The most critical thing is to ask for exactly what you want. If you want output formatted a specific way or want the model to exclude certain topics, include this in your prompt using clear, unambiguous language. For instance, instead of "what cities are near bodies of water?", ask "give me 10 cities near bodies of water, formatted in a table with their populations, countries, and areas". If you want a shorter or longer response, request it. The more specific you are, the more likely you'll get exactly what you're looking for.

Provide examples and context: Providing several good examples can significantly enhance model performance for most tasks. Referred to as few-shot or in-context learning, this allows the model to understand your task without modifying the model. Select examples that cover a wide variety of cases rather than similar examples. You can also provide relevant reference information in the prompt (in the system prompt or user text). For example, to classify which company project a meeting belongs to, include a list of projects and their descriptions in the prompt, then ask the system to use that information.

Simplify the task: Breaking complex tasks into simpler steps improves a model's ability to complete them. Use the output from a previous response as input to the next; chat completions make it easy to maintain state. For example, to determine if a forum message is appropriate, break it into determining if the message is spam/offensive, then whether it is on-topic. This breaks the task into simpler tasks and can short-circuit if the message is obviously spam or offensive, saving tokens and improving latency.

Allow the model to think: When a task requires problem solving or reasoning, chain-of-thought prompting (reasoning step by step) improves results. It is useful for logic, mathematics, coding, or reasoning problems; when narrowing several possible responses to one; when a complex output structure is necessary; and for debugging. For simple fact recall, editing existing text, or creative tasks, chain of thought may be unnecessary and only add token cost and latency. As general guidance, try writing your query without thinking, then introduce thinking if you need better results. A driving-time arithmetic example shows a wrong direct answer versus a correct step-by-step one.

Let the model call for help: LLMs are not strong at all tasks. Allow the system to use external tools instead of requiring the model to answer when not confident. For example, complex arithmetic is challenging for LLMs but trivial for a calculator; providing a calculator via tool calling dramatically improves accuracy.

Model selection

Choosing important criteria: Balance cost against capabilities. Smaller models cost less and run faster but may offer unacceptably low performance. First understand accuracy/quality requirements, then work toward cost targets. Trying a few example queries provides insufficient insight; you need performance on a representative amount of real-world data. Before experiments, document rough requirements for both cost and accuracy. You can often relax accuracy requirements by making small changes to the product or system outside the AI service.

Solve your task: Develop a small evaluation dataset to capture different models' performance. Using the most powerful model available, test a variety of prompts and few-shot examples to reach desired accuracy. If you cannot reach targets with the most powerful model, consider: using fine-tuning if you need more than a few dozen examples (more up-front work but better performance and lower costs), and using tool calling or retrieval-augmented generation to help the model retrieve relevant information.

Optimize for cost and run-time: After a working model and prompt, optimize. Starting from the larger model, use progressively smaller models to find where the model becomes too small. If you still need cheaper/faster: iterate prompting with more examples, minimize required tokens (especially output tokens, e.g., ask the model to be terse), split up or simplify the task, or distill a smaller model by collecting responses from the larger one and fine-tuning the smaller.

Evaluation

The importance of evaluation: Evaluating a model's performance is critical for making improvements or avoiding failures - you can't improve what you don't measure. Spend time and effort on evaluation from the start.

Choosing an evaluation target: Think about what behavior you want, specifying inputs, expected outputs, and what counts as correct. If you can't write these out, your problem likely isn't well defined. Select one or more metrics: Accuracy (for questions with an obvious correct answer), Mean Opinion Score (for output depending on human preferences), and Response Length (to understand if an answer is too long or short).

Selecting data to evaluate on: Select representative, unbiased test data, and expect to iterate on your test set. Ensure data is representative and unbiased, covers what you expect in the real world, and (for fine-tuned models) is not the same data used for fine-tuning. You may find existing datasets or build your own; thoroughly understand your dataset by exploring samples manually.

Scalability & performance

Latency: Response time is characterized by time to first token (the time before any initial tokens are generated; lower feels more responsive) and total runtime (time to generate the entire response). Smaller models are faster to first token and have lower total runtime. For a given model size, the largest contributor to latency is total output tokens generated, so reducing output tokens (asking the model to be terse) is the first place to focus. Input tokens matter more for time to first token but less for total runtime.

Parallelization: Parallelization can improve total runtime. For batch tasks, distribute the job across multiple API calls. You can parallelize a single request by breaking the task into smaller parts (e.g., generate 5 example documents in parallel), or do part of the task in parallel (e.g., OCR documents in parallel, then analyze the combined data in a single request).

Moderation

Automated moderation: Llama is trained with safety in mind but you may need additional protection. Use the moderations endpoint to automatically moderate problematic content.

System prompts: The system prompt guides output but should not be relied on to protect against unsafe outputs, as the model can be convinced to work around constraints. Add hard-coded checks after the model runs if certain words/phrases must not be output. Do not consider your system prompt safely hidden, and do not include sensitive or confidential information in it.

Designing for mistakes: Llama sometimes makes mistakes; design your system to be robust to error. Present a confirmation to the user rather than directly using output to make a decision, warn users that output may be incorrect, and offer users the ability to give feedback.

Adversarial testing: Actively test your system under pressure (red teaming) to deliberately produce incorrect outputs, bypass filters, or break the model. Save and reuse adversarial prompts for regression testing.

Chat completion

Llama API is currently available as a preview release, with ongoing changes to API endpoints, parameters and models.

The chat completion endpoint generates chat completions for conversation threads using Llama models. This endpoint supports both standard completion requests and integrated tool workflows, with optional server-sent event (SSE) streaming for streaming responses.

See chat completion, image understanding, structured output and tool calling for more details on chat completion features, and learn techniques for using chat completion in production in the chat and conversation guide.

POST /chat/completions

Generate a chat completion for the given messages using the specified model.

Request body (Content Type: application/json):
- model (string, required): model id
- messages (array of UserMessage, SystemMessage, AssistantMessage, ToolResponseMessage, required): messages
- response_format (one of ResponseFormatJsonSchema, ResponseFormatText, optional): response format
- store (boolean, optional): Whether or not to store the output of this chat completion request as JSON in our manifold bucket
- stream (boolean, optional): stream
- tools (array, optional): tools
- tool_choice (one of string, ChatCompletionNamedToolChoice, optional): Controls which (if any) tool is called by the model. "none" means the model will not call any tool and instead generates a message. "auto" means the model can pick between generating a message or calling one or more tools. "required" means the model must call one or more tools. Specifying a particular tool via {"type": "function", "function":{"name": "my_function"}} forces the model to call that tool. "none" is the default when no tools are present; "auto" is the default if tools are present.
- repetition_penalty (number, optional): repetition penalty
- temperature (number, optional): temperature
- top_p (number, optional): top p
- top_k (integer, optional): top k
- max_completion_tokens (integer, optional): max tokens
- logprobs (boolean, optional): Whether to return log probabilities of the output tokens or not. If true, returns the log probabilities of each output token returned in the content of message
- top_logprobs (integer, optional): An integer between 0 and 20 specifying the number of most likely tokens to return at each token position, each with an associated log probability. logprobs must be set to true if this parameter is used.
- user (string, optional): A unique identifier representing your end-user to monitor and detect abuse.
- reasoning_effort (enum: 'minimal', 'low', 'medium', 'high', 'xhigh', 'max', optional): Constrains effort on reasoning for reasoning models.
- stop (array, optional): List of strings that will stop generation when encountered.

Response

HTTP 200 - Full chat completion response (Content Type: application/json):
- id (string, required): response id
- completion_message (object, required): completion message
- logprobs (object, optional): logprobs
- metrics (array, optional): metrics

Content Type: text/event-stream:
- id (string, required): response id
- event (object, required): streaming response event

Example (curl):

  curl -X POST https://api.llama.com/v1/chat/completions \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $LLAMA_API_KEY" \
  -d '{
    "model": "Llama-4-Maverick-17B-128E-Instruct-FP8",
    "messages": [
      {"role": "user", "content": "Hello, how are you?"}
    ],
    "max_completion_tokens": 1024,
    "temperature": 0.7
  }'

Code samples are available for curl, Python, Python (Llama API client), Python (OpenAI client), TypeScript (Llama API client), and Shell.

Llama API Data Commitments

Meta's responsible innovation principles serve as the foundation for all our work. These principles are specifically crafted to protect people's privacy so they feel empowered to explore, connect and engage with our products.

Meta does not train its AI models on Llama API Customer Content or Customer Data.

- Customer Data comprises your account data, roles, and profile fields.
- Customer Content comprises both the inputs you submit to the model (prompts) and the outputs you receive based on your inputs (model responses).

Your Customer Content and Customer Data are used only:
1. To provide Llama API services.
2. To understand how our services are used.
3. To ensure adherence to the Acceptable Use Policy.
4. To comply with legal obligations.

Your Customer Content and your Customer Data are not used for any purposes other than those described in our permitted purposes. Customer Content and Customer Data are not used for personalization of consumer Meta Products or advertising, and personal data collected from the use of Llama API products is not used to personalize ads.

Your Customer Content and Customer Data are logically separated except when shared to enforce the AUP, to facilitate payments, or to comply with other legal or regulatory requirements. Your Customer Content and Customer Data are always stored subject to strict access controls, and Meta will not sell any customer or user data as defined in the Terms of Service.

Encryption

All data transmitted between Llama API and backend servers is encrypted with the industry-standard TLS 1.2 and TLS 1.3 protocols.

Meta encrypts Customer Content and specific Customer Data when it is stored at rest, except in limited circumstances as described below. We encrypt your data at rest before it is persisted in storage. Specifically, this data is encrypted at rest using strong symmetric encryption algorithms such as ChaCha20-Poly1305 (XChaPoly) and AES-GCM.

All Customer Content is encrypted when it's stored at rest, except when required to comply with legal obligations. Examples:
- API "inputs" or "prompts"
- API "outputs" or "responses"
- Parameters that are added in API code, including configuration parameters

The specific Customer Data listed below are encrypted when stored at rest, except (i) when required to comply with legal obligations, (ii) to ensure adherence to our Acceptable Use Policy, or (iii) when customers submit this information to interact with customer support.
- User profile/account information:
  - Name
  - Role/Permission
  - Location
  - Mobile phone number, except when used to send an SMS message to the person
  - Email address, and email addresses of invited collaborators except when used to send an email notification to the person
  - Date of birth

Payment Data

Meta processes all payment card data according to the Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard (PCI-DSS). Payment card numbers are securely stored, encrypted at rest, and stored separately from your profile data. The data provided to facilitate payments within Llama API is used only to provide billing services and is never used for personalization of consumer Meta Products or advertising.

Meta's investments in Security

Meta performs regular security and vulnerability testing to assess whether key controls are properly implemented and effective. Meta has a vulnerability management program that includes definition of roles and responsibilities, dedicated ownership of vulnerability monitoring, vulnerability risk assessment and patch deployment.

Meta's security team is responsible for the detection, triage and remediation of vulnerabilities in Meta's hardware and software. Meta leverages various tools to detect security bugs in its code base, as well as in open-source and third-party code, in order to mitigate or fix security bugs before they make it into shipped Meta's products and impact our customers.

Llama API benefits from Meta's commitment to the security of your data which manifests through the monitoring, controls and measures we have in place to pre-empt or respond to security risks.

Managing the security lifecycle

Meta has established and will maintain an Information Security Management System (ISMS) designed to implement industry-standard information security practices. Meta's ISMS is designed to protect against unauthorized access, disclosure, use, loss or alteration of Customer Data.

Meta has a security incident response plan for monitoring, detecting and handling possible incidents. The plan includes the definition of roles and responsibilities, communication protocols and post mortem reviews, including root cause analysis and remediation plans. Meta monitors the service for any security breaches and malicious activity. The monitoring process and detection techniques are designed to detect security incidents according to relevant threats and ongoing threat intelligence.

For each account, the concurrency limits for different DeepSeek API models are shown in the table below.

# Error Codes

When calling the DeepSeek API, you may encounter errors. The causes and solutions are listed below.

400 - Invalid Format. Cause: invalid request body format. Solution: modify your request body according to the hints in the error message.
401 - Authentication Fails. Cause: authentication fails due to the wrong API key. Solution: check your API key, or create one if you do not have it.
402 - Insufficient Balance. Cause: you have run out of balance. Solution: check your account balance and go to the Top up page to add funds.
422 - Invalid Parameters. Cause: your request contains invalid parameters. Solution: modify your request parameters according to the hints in the error message.
429 - Rate Limit Reached. Cause: you are sending requests too quickly. Solution: pace your requests reasonably, or temporarily switch to an alternative provider.
500 - Server Error. Cause: our server encounters an issue. Solution: retry after a brief wait and contact support if the issue persists.
503 - Server Overloaded. Cause: the server is overloaded due to high traffic. Solution: retry your request after a brief wait.

A 402 signals an exhausted balance and directs the user to top up funds. A 422 flags invalid parameters that need adjusting. A 429 means requests are sent too quickly, advising users to pace them or temporarily fall back to another provider. The purpose is to help developers diagnose and resolve failed API calls quickly.

# Thinking Mode

The DeepSeek model supports the thinking mode: before outputting the final answer, the model will first output a chain-of-thought reasoning to improve the accuracy of the final response.

## Thinking Mode Toggle and Effort Control

Control parameters:
- Thinking Mode Toggle (OpenAI Format): {"thinking": {"type": "enabled/disabled"}}
- Thinking Effort Control (OpenAI Format): {"reasoning_effort": "high/max"}
- Thinking Effort Control (Anthropic Format): {"output_config": {"effort": "high/max"}}

(1) The thinking toggle defaults to `enabled`
(2) In thinking mode, the default effort is `high` for regular requests; for some complex agent requests (such as Claude Code, OpenCode), effort is automatically set to `max`
(3) In thinking mode, for compatibility, `low` and `medium` are mapped to `high`, and `xhigh` is mapped to `max`

When using the OpenAI SDK, you need to pass the `thinking` parameter within `extra_body`:

## Input and Output Parameters

Thinking mode does not support the `temperature`, `top_p`, `presence_penalty`, or `frequency_penalty` parameters. Please note that, for compatibility with existing software, setting these parameters will not trigger an error but will also have no effect.

In thinking mode, the chain-of-thought content is returned via the `reasoning_content` parameter, at the same level as `content`. When concatenating subsequent turns, you can selectively return `reasoning_content` to the API:

- Between two `user` messages, if the model did not perform a tool call, the intermediate `assistant`'s `reasoning_content` does not need to participate in the context concatenation. If passed to the API in subsequent turns, it will be ignored.
- Between two `user` messages, if the model performed a tool call, the intermediate `assistant`'s `reasoning_content` must participate in the context concatenation and must be passed back to the API in all subsequent user interaction turns.

## Multi-turn Conversation

In each turn of the conversation, the model outputs the CoT (`reasoning_content`) and the final answer (`content`). If there is no tool call, the CoT content from previous turns will not be concatenated into the context in the next turn.

The DeepSeek model's thinking mode supports tool calls. Before outputting the final answer, the model can perform multiple turns of reasoning and tool calls to improve the quality of the response.

Please note that, unlike turns in thinking mode that do not involve tool calls, for turns that do perform tool calls, the `reasoning_content` must be fully passed back to the API in all subsequent requests.

If your code does not correctly pass back `reasoning_content`, the API will return a 400 error.

# JSON Output

In many scenarios, users need the model to output in strict JSON format to achieve structured output, facilitating subsequent parsing.

DeepSeek provides JSON Output to ensure the model outputs valid JSON strings.

## Notice

To enable JSON Output, users should:

1. Set the `response_format` parameter to `{'type': 'json_object'}`.
2. Include the word "json" in the system or user prompt, and provide an example of the desired JSON format to guide the model in outputting valid JSON.
3. Set the `max_tokens` parameter reasonably to prevent the JSON string from being truncated midway.

# Tool Calls

Tool Calls allows the model to call external tools to enhance its capabilities.

## Non-thinking Mode

### Sample Code

Here is an example of using Tool Calls to get the current weather information of the user's location, demonstrated with complete Python code. For the specific API format of Tool Calls, please refer to the Chat Completion documentation.

The execution flow of this example is as follows:

1. User: Asks about the current weather in Hangzhou
2. Model: Returns the function `get_weather({location: 'Hangzhou'})`
3. User: Calls the function `get_weather({location: 'Hangzhou'})` and provides the result to the model
4. Model: Returns in natural language, "The current temperature in Hangzhou is 24°C."

Note: In the above code, the functionality of the `get_weather` function needs to be provided by the user. The model itself does not execute specific functions.

## Thinking Mode

From DeepSeek-V3.2, the API supports tool use in the thinking mode. For more details, please refer to Thinking Mode.

## `strict` Mode (Beta)

In `strict` mode, the model strictly adheres to the format requirements of the Function's JSON schema when outputting a tool call, ensuring that the model's output complies with the user's definition. It is supported by both thinking and non-thinking mode.

To use `strict` mode, you need to:

1. Use `base_url="https://api.deepseek.com/beta"` to enable Beta features
2. In the `tools` parameter, all `function` need to set the `strict` property to `true`
3. The server will validate the JSON Schema of the Function provided by the user. If the schema does not conform to the specifications or contains JSON schema types that are not supported by the server, an error message will be returned

Example strict-mode tool definition sets "strict": true and "additionalProperties": false on the parameters object.

### Supported Json Schema Types In `strict` Mode

- object: All properties of every object must be set as required, and additionalProperties must be set to false.
- string: Supported parameters pattern and format (email, hostname, ipv4, ipv6, uuid). Unsupported: minLength, maxLength.
- number/integer: Supported parameters const, default, minimum, maximum, exclusiveMinimum, exclusiveMaximum, multipleOf.
- array: Unsupported parameters minItems, maxItems.
- enum: Ensures output is one of predefined options.
- anyOf: Matches any one of the provided schemas, allowing fields to accommodate multiple valid formats.
- $ref and $def: Use $def to define reusable modules and $ref to reference them, reducing schema repetition and enabling modularization; $ref can also define recursive structures.

# Context Caching

The DeepSeek API Context Caching on Disk Technology is enabled by default for all users, allowing them to benefit without needing to modify their code.

Each user request will trigger the construction of a hard disk cache. If subsequent requests have overlapping prefixes with previous requests, the overlapping part will only be fetched from the cache, which counts as a "cache hit."

## Cache Persistence and Hit Rules

A cache hit requires that the corresponding prefix has already been "persisted" (written to the disk cache). Due to the Sliding Window Attention mechanism, the storage and matching of cached prefixes differs from before. Each cached prefix is an independent, complete unit. A subsequent request can only hit the cache if it fully matches a cache prefix unit.

### When cache prefixes are persisted:

1. Persistence at request boundaries: Each request will produce two cache prefix units at the end position of the user input and the end position of the model output. A subsequent request can hit the cache if it fully matches them.

2. Common prefix detection persistence: When the system detects a common prefix across multiple requests, it will persist that common prefix as an independent cache prefix unit. A subsequent request can hit the cache if it fully reuses that cache prefix unit.

3. Persistence at fixed token intervals: For long inputs or long outputs, the system will carve out cache prefix units at fixed token intervals, to avoid long prefixes from being completely uncacheable due to never reaching an end position.

Example 1: A user's first-round request is `A + B`, and the second-round request is `A + B + C`. The second request can fully match the cache prefix unit `A + B`, hitting the cache for `A + B`.

Example 2: A user's first-round request is `A + B`, and the second-round request is `A + C`. The second request cannot hit the cache, because `A + C` does not fully match the first round's cache prefix unit (`A + B`). However, at this point the system will detect that the two requests share a common prefix `A`, and persist `A` as a cache prefix unit. When a third-round request `A + D` arrives, it can fully match the cache prefix unit `A`, hitting the cache for `A`.

### Example 2: Long Text Q&A

First Request, Second Request, and Third Request share a system message plus financial report content. The first two requests will not hit the cache. After they complete, the system will identify the system message + financial report content in the user message as a cache prefix unit and persist it. In the third request, since it fully matches the previously persisted cache prefix unit, it can hit the cache.

## Checking Cache Hit Status

In the response from the DeepSeek API, two fields in the `usage` section reflect the cache hit status of the request:

1. `prompt_cache_hit_tokens`: The number of tokens in the input of this request that resulted in a cache hit.
2. `prompt_cache_miss_tokens`: The number of tokens in the input of this request that did not result in a cache hit.

## Hard Disk Cache and Output Randomness

The hard disk cache only matches the prefix part of the user's input. The output is still generated through computation and inference, and it is influenced by parameters such as temperature, introducing randomness.

## Additional Notes

1. The cache system works on a "best-effort" basis and does not guarantee a 100% cache hit rate.
2. Cache construction takes seconds. Once the cache is no longer in use, it will be automatically cleared, usually within a few hours to a few days.

With simple configuration, you can integrate the capabilities of DeepSeek into the Anthropic API ecosystem.

Note: When you pass an unsupported model name to DeepSeek's Anthropic API, the API backend will automatically map it to the `deepseek-v4-flash` model.

## Anthropic Model Mapping

When you use the Anthropic API, we map the Claude model names you pass in:

- Models starting with claude-opus are mapped to deepseek-v4-pro
- Models starting with claude-haiku or claude-sonnet are mapped to deepseek-v4-flash

With this mapping, when using the developer mode of the new Claude Desktop APP, you can bypass the APP's model name restrictions by simply changing the base_url and api_key to connect to DeepSeek models.
